newsitem.title: GERMANY: Million pack Cologne centre for Rose Monday parade.
newsitem.headline: Million pack Cologne centre for Rose Monday parade.

text.p: A million revellers clad as clowns, convicts and candy-throwing cavaliers crowded central Cologne for the traditional Rose Monday parade, capping the carnival season with one of the world's biggest costume parties.

More than one million brightly dressed spectators lined up 30 deep on Monday to watch some 8,000 costumed figures parade on 74 floats along a 6.5-km (four-mile) route through the centre of the mediaeval city.

With a huge national audience following the festival live on television, the exuberant crowds sang and danced to the music of 111 bands, locking arms as they weaved back and forth in patterns that often blurred the divisions between watchers and marchers.

Dressed in a myriad costumes as 18th century wig-clad warriors, 21st century space travellers or the ubiquitous capped fool, revellers from around Germany and across Europe flocked to Cologne, a city of 940,000 whose population doubles each year for the "Rosenmontag" parade.

"Cologne is the only city in Germany that really knows how to enjoy life," said Frank Krueger, a 32-year-old hi-fi salesman wearing a pirate costume. "We turn a little Brazilian today. It's great that people stop taking things so seriously for a day."

In a country not normally noted for its abandon, the Rose Monday parade marks the climax to the carnival season that started on November 11. After this last week of nearly non-stop partying in Cologne the season officially ends on Ash Wednesday.

"You have to be careful you don't drink too much because you can very easily end up sleeping right through the next day," said Frank Hackenberg, a 32-year-old university professor, while drinking the popular local Koelsch beer.
The four-hour-long parade, which formally starts at 11.11 a.m., actually begins hours before and ends hours later.

But local residents warn visitors that parade-watching in Cologne is not a passive activity, telling guests in a brochure: "If you were at the procession and saw the procession, then you weren't at the procession."
Erwin Metzler, a 45-year-old electrician who travelled 500 km (300 miles) from the Black Forest town of Ravensburg, said he had never seen so much singing, kissing, dancing and frolicking.
"It's a really wild thing here in Cologne," he said. "The whole city has gone crazy."

Whether running hand in hand around groups of on-duty police officers or tossing tonnes of candy and flowers into the crowd, the "Jecken" (fools) moved slowly forward on streets covered by a steady downpour of confetti.
"It's the best party of the year," said Siegfried Lorenz, a 52-year-old tax adviser dressed as a pig.

Many of the elaborate flower-covered floats lampooned political leaders, with burly Chancellor Helmut Kohl a favourite target. Floats and banners ridiculed Kohl for raising taxes, cutting expenditure and high unemployment.
But many of the participants had more modest political aims.

"We are campaigning for more protection for frogs during mating season," said Niki Michelts, a 25-year-old office worker who was leading a group wearing bright green frog costumes. "We need to make the world a safer place for the frogs."
